title: Structural motif discovery over the symbol/call/import graph
description:
Find small (3–5 node) connected subgraphs that occur in the sutra symbol/call/import graph **significantly more often than in a randomized null-model graph**. Goal: surface recurring structural patterns and anti-patterns ("module exposes type → trait impl in same module → consumer in sibling module"; circular sibling references; over-coupled facade modules).

Reference: Milo et al., "Network Motifs: Simple Building Blocks of Complex Networks" (2002). Tools: gtrieScanner, FANMOD; or roll our own — algorithm is straightforward (enumerate small subgraphs, count, compare to null).

Why this over PH: motifs are *interpretable* — a 4-node diagram with "happens 47× more than chance" tells a story. PH persistence diagrams don't.

Design questions to grill before building:
- Which graph: call graph, import graph, type-uses graph, or a unified multigraph?
- Null model: configuration model (preserve degree distribution), edge-swap, or uniform random? Different choices give different "significant" motifs.
- Motif size: 3 only? 3+4? 3+4+5? Combinatorics blow up fast.
- Directed or undirected? sutra's edges are directed; preserving that matters.
- Statistical significance threshold (Z-score? p-value with how many null samples?).
- Output: report skill, MCP tool, or stored as an analyzable artifact?

acceptance_criteria.text: Prototype run on the manas codebase yields at least one interpretable pattern (or a clear negative result)
Decision made on whether to ship as feature or close as research-only
